notes.meaning: Samson traveled down to the Philistine town of Timnah and saw a young Philistine woman who caught his attention. He went home to ask his parents to arrange the marriage for him, which was the custom of the time. While his desire was driven simply by what he saw, he did show proper honor by asking for his father and mother's blessing and help.

Samson's parents objected to his choice, urging him to marry an Israelite woman instead of someone from the ungodly Philistines. Samson insisted, replying that she looked right to his eyes. He chose to follow his own sight and strong impulses rather than the wise guidance of his father and mother.

His parents did not realize that the Lord was using this situation to begin breaking the Philistines' harsh rule over Israel. God used Samson's private desires and choices to create an opportunity to strike back at the oppressors. Even human mistakes do not stop God from working out his plans of deliverance.

On the journey down to Timnah, Samson went into the vineyards and was attacked by a roaring, full-grown young lion. The Spirit of the Lord suddenly gave him supernatural power, enabling him to tear the wild beast apart with his bare hands. He kept the deed entirely secret from his parents, showing genuine humility after an amazing display of God's strength.

Samson reached Timnah and spoke with the young woman, and his conversation confirmed that he liked her. His parents' involvement helped pave the way for the formal engagement. Once again, he moved forward with the match because she pleased his eyes.

Some time later, Samson traveled back to Timnah to marry the woman and turned off the path to look at the dead lion. The hot sun had dried out the carcass, and a swarm of bees had made a hive with honey inside the rib cage. This unusual sight later provided the idea for Samson's famous riddle.

Samson scooped up some honey in his hands and ate it along the road, sharing some with his parents when he caught up to them. He never told them where he got it, knowing they would object to food taken from an unclean dead animal. Even so, he showed care for his father and mother by letting them taste the treat he had found.

Samson's father went down to Timnah for the wedding, and Samson hosted a seven-day banquet as was normal for young men at that time. Even as a set-apart servant of God, he joined in the common social festivities of the culture. A good wedding feast was meant to be a time of shared joy and hospitality.

Because Samson had come without his own groomsmen, the Philistines provided thirty young men from the town to attend him. While they were sent to show honor at the feast, they also served as watchful guards over this unusually strong stranger. Friendly gestures from enemies can sometimes hide deeper suspicion.

Samson proposed a riddle to his thirty guests to entertain the wedding company, which was a popular custom at festive gatherings. He wagered thirty fine linen garments and thirty changes of clothing on whether they could solve it before the seven days of feasting ended. The guests accepted the challenge, eager to test their wits against the groom.

Samson gave them his riddle: food came out of an eater, and something sweet came out of something strong. The guests spent three days puzzling over the words, but they could not find the answer. The riddle was grounded in Samson's private encounter with the lion, which made it impossible for them to guess without insider knowledge.

Fearing humiliation and financial loss, the Philistine men turned on Samson's bride with terrifying threats. They ordered her to coax the secret out of her new husband, warning that they would burn her and her family's house down if she failed. Their violent response revealed the cruelty and greed hidden beneath their festive manners.

Terrified by the threats, Samson's bride wept before him and accused him of not loving her because he kept the secret to himself. Samson defended himself by pointing out that he had not even told his own parents, who had known him all his life. He found himself caught between his personal loyalty and his wife's desperate pleas.

The bride continued her tears and begging throughout the feast until Samson finally gave in on the seventh day because she pressed him so hard. As soon as he revealed the answer, she went straight to her Philistine countrymen and told them. Samson's physical strength was vast, but he proved vulnerable to emotional pressure.

Just before sunset on the last day, the men gave Samson the answer by asking what was sweeter than honey and stronger than a lion. Samson answered with a sharp proverb, declaring that they would never have solved it if they had not used his wife to get the secret. Though he knew they had cheated, he still honored the wager.

differ.view: Some read the proverb as pointing to his wife's marital infidelity and attachment to his rivals, while others take it simply as an idiom for using his wife to coax out the answer.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church teachers saw the riddle as a sacred mystery pointing to Christ, who brought sweetness and safety out of death and bitterness for all nations.

notes.meaning: The Spirit of the Lord empowered Samson with strength and courage, and he went down to the Philistine city of Ashkelon, struck down thirty men, took their fine clothes, and paid off his wager. Furious over how he had been betrayed, he left his bride behind and returned home to his father's house. God used this painful dispute to ignite a conflict between Samson and Israel's oppressors.

After Samson left in anger, his bride's family gave her away in marriage to the man who had served as his best man during the wedding. The family treated the marriage as over instead of trying to heal the breach, making the division permanent. This act of betrayal finished cutting Samson's ties with the Philistines.
